title: A .vimrc that helps
summary: The dozen settings worth having everywhere, and how vim reads them.

steps.title: ~/.vimrc
body: vim reads `~/.vimrc` (neovim: `~/.config/nvim/init.vim` or `init.lua`) at start-up. Every line is an Ex command without the colon. A small, server-friendly one:
set relativenumber     " ...relative to the cursor line, for 5j / d3k
set expandtab          " Tab key inserts spaces
set shiftwidth=4       " >> and auto-indent use 4 spaces
set tabstop=4          " a real tab character displays as 4 columns
set incsearch          " jump to matches while you type /pattern
set hlsearch           " highlight all matches (:noh to clear)
set ignorecase smartcase   " case-insensitive unless you type a capital
`"` starts a comment. Try a setting live first with `:set number`, then add it to the file. `:set number?` shows the current value; `:set nonumber` (or `:set number!`) turns it off.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: Match the setting to what it does.
pairs: number lines by distance from the cursor
highlight every match of the last search
move to matches while typing the pattern

steps.prompt: Your YAML file fails to parse after you indented it in vim with Tab. Which setting fixes it for next time?
steps.explain: YAML forbids tab characters for indentation. `expandtab` makes Tab insert spaces; `:retab` converts tabs already in the file.

steps.prompt: With `set number relativenumber`, the cursor is on line 12. What number is shown in the gutter of line 15, and of line 12 itself? Answer like `a b`.
steps.explain: Other lines show their distance (`3`); the cursor line shows its absolute number when `number` is also on.

steps.prompt: Boolean switch or setting with a value?
Turn off search highlighting in the vimrc and set the indent width to 2.
steps.explain: Prefix a boolean option with `no` to turn it off.

steps.title: Where settings come from
body: `:verbose set shiftwidth?` tells you the value **and the file that set it**, which is how you find out a plugin or `ftplugin` overrode your vimrc.

Order of loading: system vimrc (`/etc/vim/vimrc`), your `~/.vimrc`, then plugins, then filetype plugins when a file opens. Later wins. For one-off files, a **modeline** at the top or bottom of the file can set options too: `# vim: set ts=2 sw=2 et:`.

steps.prompt: You put `set shiftwidth=4` in `~/.vimrc`, but in Python files `>>` indents by 8. How do you find the culprit?
steps.explain: `:verbose` adds *Last set from <file>* to the answer.

steps.title: Read a vimrc
prompt: Write `Dictionary<string, string> ReadVimrc(string[] lines)` returning the final value of every option set by `set` lines:
- ignore blank lines and lines whose first non-blank character is `"` (comments); ignore lines that do not start with `set `.
- a line can set several options: `set ignorecase smartcase`.
- `name=value` stores `value`; `name` stores `"true"`; `noname` stores `"false"` for `name`; `name!` flips the current value (missing counts as `"false"`).
- later lines win. Text after a `"` that follows whitespace is a trailing comment.
solution: opts[name] = opts.TryGetValue(name, out var v) && v == "true" ? "false" : "true";
hints: Strip trailing comments by cutting at the first `" ` preceded by a space.
Split the rest of a `set` line on spaces and handle each item: `=`, trailing `!`, `no` prefix, plain.
template: Dojo.Eq("toggle of an unset option", "true", dojoRc["incsearch"]);
Dojo.Eq("syntax is not a set line", false, dojoRc.ContainsKey("syntax"));
